infons.kwd: Hygiene practice Complementary feeding Systematic review Meta-analysis

passages.text: Ethiopia hygiene practice during complementary feeding and associated factors; systematic review and meta-analysis
Background

Complementary feeding is crucial for infant growth, but poor hygiene during this period increases the risk of malnutrition and illness. In Ethiopia, national data on hygiene practices during complementary feeding, particularly among mothers of children aged 6-24 months, is limited. This study aims to synthesize existing data through a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the status of hygiene practices and identify key influencing factors, informing public health strategies to improve child health outcomes.
Methods

The systematic review methods were defined following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. A search strategy was implemented using electronic databases (Medline, Global Health, Google Scholar, Web of Science, Embase, CINAHL, and Psyc INFO) as well as grey literature. The Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal checklist was used to assess the quality of the studies. The meta-analysis was conducted using STATA 17 software to compute pooled prevalence and odds ratios (OR) for the determinant factors, with a 95% confidence interval (CI).
Results

The systematic review and meta-analysis included six studies with 2,565 mothers. The overall pooled prevalence of hygienic practices during complementary feeding was 42% (95% CI: 35%-48%). Subgroup analysis showed a prevalence of 41% in southern Ethiopia and 39% in northern Ethiopia. Significant factors associated with better hygiene practices included having hand washing facilities near toilets (AOR: 4.6, 95% CI: 1.04-8.31, p = 0.01) and a positive attitude towards hygiene (AOR: 2.7, 95% CI: 1.07-4.69, p < 0.05).
Conclusions

This systematic review and meta-analysis found a low proportion of hygienic practices during complementary feeding in Ethiopia, with maternal attitude and access to hand washing facilities identified as key predictors. Training and counseling for mothers on safe food processing are recommended, along with further research on community interventions and the impact of socio-economic factors on hygiene practices.
Supplementary Information
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12887-024-05319-4.
Background

The World Health Organization (WHO) defines complementary feeding (CF) as a process that starts when breast milk alone is no longer sufficient to meet the nutritional requirements of the infant. An infant's need for energy and nutrients exceeds that provided by breast milk at six months of age. The two years following the end of exclusive breastfeeding are crucial windows for a child's growth and development. Although breastfeeding begins at six months, it should be combined with safe, age-appropriate solid, semisolid, and soft foods that are stored and prepared hygienically and fed with clean hands.

According to the guidelines for infant and young child feeding indicators, complementary foods should be prepared, stored, and fed with clean hands and utensils rather than bottles and teat feedings. This transition from exclusive breastfeeding to family foods is a critical period during which poor hygiene practices in complementary feeding significantly contribute to the high prevalence of gastrointestinal and respiratory illnesses in young children. Gastrointestinal diseases associated with preventable food-borne bacteria remain a global health challenge for children under two years of age, as their immature immune systems make them particularly vulnerable to infections with enteric pathogens.

Inappropriate feeding practices can lead to malnutrition in young children. Those who lack proper nutrition are more likely to develop infections, experience poor growth, and die nearly six times more often. Approximately 600 million food-borne diseases are diagnosed worldwide annually, resulting in 420,000 deaths. Children under five account for 30% of these food-borne deaths, with more than 125,000 children in this age group dying each year from such diseases.

Infectious diseases caused by enteric pathogens associated with preventable food-borne bacteria remain a major global health threat for children under the age of two. Furthermore, dietary contamination results in diarrheal diseases that cause approximately 230,000 deaths every year. Poor food hygiene practices contribute to 70% of diarrhea episodes in developing countries, leading to 88% of childhood deaths. The process of feeding complementary foods is directly related to malnutrition, which is estimated to be the underlying cause of 45% of all deaths in children under five years of age; 41% of these deaths occur in sub-Saharan Africa, and 34% occur in South Asia.

The transmission of food-borne diseases among children is exacerbated by unsafe food-handling practices by mothers and caregivers. Approximately 10% to 20% of food-borne disease outbreaks are attributed to unclean food preparation practices by mothers. The current prevalence of adequate complementary food introduction in Ethiopia is 13%, according to the 2019 Mini Demographic and Health Survey. Additionally, preventable bacterial pathogens are responsible for 43% of infant mortalities.

Several interventions have been implemented in Africa and Ethiopia to improve hygiene practices during complementary feeding. These interventions include community-based health education programs that focus on the importance of hand washing before food preparation and feeding. For example, programs that distribute hygiene kits and provide training sessions for mothers and caregivers on safe food handling practices have demonstrated effectiveness in reducing food-borne illnesses among young children. Initiatives that promote the use of clean utensils and hygienic food storage are crucial for enhancing hygiene standards among caregivers.

Despite these efforts, there is a scarcity of national evidence on the status of hygiene practices during complementary feeding, particularly among mothers of children aged 6-24 months, who often face challenges such as busy work schedules that limit their attention to food hygiene practices. The current study aims to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis to derive reliable and current figures regarding the hygiene practices during complementary feeding in Ethiopia.
Methods
Search strategy

The systematic review methods were defined following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines and were registered in PROSPERO (CRD42024498118). A search strategy was implemented using electronic databases (Medline, Global Health, Google Scholar, Web of Science, Embase, CINAHL, and PsycINFO), while a grey literature search was conducted, no relevant articles were identified from that source. The search strategy was initially developed in Medline using MeSH subject headings combined with free-text terms related to the four search components: "hygiene practice," "complementary feeding," "associated factors," and "mothers." This strategy was then adapted for use in the other databases, covering studies published from January 1, 2013, to December 1, 2023. Additionally, further studies were retrieved through manual reference listing of included studies, relevant reviews, and consultations with experts in the field.
Eligibility criteria
Inclusion criteria
Study Design: Cross-sectional studies, cohort studies, case control studies or interventional studies.
Population: Studies involving mothers of children aged 6-24 months in Ethiopia.

Intervention/Exposure: Studies that assess hygiene practices during complementary feeding, including but not limited to hand washing practices, hygiene of feeding utensils, and food preparation hygiene.
Outcome Measures: Studies reporting on the prevalence of hygienic practices or factors influencing hygiene practices.
Language: Studies published in English.
Publication Date: Studies published from January 1, 2013, to December 1, 2023.
Exclusion criteria
Study Design: Qualitative studies, reviews, editorials, and opinion papers.
Population: Studies focusing on populations outside Ethiopia or mothers of children younger than 6 months or older than 24 months.
Outcome Measures: Studies not reporting relevant hygiene practices or not providing sufficient data on the prevalence or factors associated with hygiene practices.
Language: Studies published in languages other than English.
Studies unavailable as full-text articles were excluded.
Outcome definition
"Hygiene practice" was defined as actions taken to ensure food safety and cleanliness during the preparation and feeding of complementary foods, which may vary across studies.
Study selection procedures

The EndNote X9 citation manager was used to import studies from various sources and remove duplicates. Five review authors (EG, EKB, GAA, KS, and GL) independently evaluated the inclusion of all potential studies identified during the search process. Other review authors (ANY, AYB, AGB, and SKB) assessed the full text of the papers to determine eligibility for final inclusion in this study. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion. Ultimately, all qualifying papers with complete contents were reviewed.

A breakdown of the number of articles retrieved from each database is as follows: Medline yielded 39 articles, Global Health contributed 400 articles, Google Scholar returned 800 articles, and Web of Science provided 600 articles. Additionally, Embase yielded 400 articles, CINAHL contributed 200 articles, and Psyc INFO provided 126 articles. In total, 2565 articles were retrieved across all databases.
Data extraction and management

After studies were imported to EndNote v.9 and duplicates were removed, three independent reviewers (EGD, EKB, and GAA) extracted essential data independently using a standardized pre-specified data abstraction format. This format was designed to minimize disagreements in the extraction process. Any discrepancies were discussed, and if necessary, the second author of the study was consulted. The data abstraction format included the author, publication year, study design, study location, sample size, participants, magnitude, and associated factors (adjusted odds ratio with confidence intervals for the variables).
Quality assessment and risk of bias

To ensure the quality and reliability of the studies included in this review, we conducted a thorough quality assessment using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist for Qualitative Research. This checklist is freely available at the JBI Critical Appraisal Tools and provides a structured approach to assess the quality of qualitative research.

The review team (SKB, GL, and ANY) employed a blinded review approach to evaluate each study's quality independently. Any discrepancies in the quality assessment were resolved through consultation with a second author (EKB). We considered studies that scored 5 or more on the JBI criteria as having good quality and eligible for inclusion in the review.

In addition to the quality assessment, we also conducted a risk of bias evaluation for each study. The JBI checklist helped identify key areas where potential bias may occur, such as in sampling methods, data collection techniques, and participant representation. Studies with a low risk of bias were prioritized in the final analysis, while studies with high or unclear risk were carefully examined for their impact on the review's findings.
Statistical analysis and data synthesis

The extracted data were entered into Microsoft Excel V.2016 and subsequently exported to STATA version 17 software for analysis. Descriptive analyses were conducted to summarize the characteristics of the included studies in summary tables and narrative text. Meta-analysis was performed, calculating the pooled estimate for the magnitude of physical activity using random-effects models with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Statistical heterogeneity was assessed both subjectively, through visual inspection of forest plots, and objectively, using the Cochrane Q-test and I2 statistics. Subgroup analyses were conducted based on sample size, publication year, and study area. The presence of publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots and Egger's and Begg's statistical tests.
Heterogeneity across studies

To evaluate heterogeneity among the reported proportions, p-values from the I-squared test were computed. Significant heterogeneity was found among the included studies in this analysis (I2 = 92.34%, p < 0.001). Consequently, the pooled effects were estimated using a random-effects meta-analysis approach based on DerSimonian and Laird.
Additional analysis

To identify potential moderating factors that might account for variations in effect sizes among the primary studies, a subgroup analysis was conducted based on various characteristics, such as publication year, sample size, and study area. Furthermore, a meta-regression model was employed to investigate the sources of heterogeneity by utilizing the sample size, study area, and publication year of each study.
Result
Study characteristics
PRISMA flow diagram for selecting the studies for the review

A total of 2565 articles from pre-selected database sources were manually searched. Duplication resulted in the removal of 705 articles. After that, 989 of them were eliminated after a review of the abstract and title. After 874 papers were assessed in their entirety, six of them qualified for a systemic review and meta-analysis (Fig. 1).

The studies included in our systematic review and meta-analysis investigated hygiene practices during complementary feeding across diverse regions in Ethiopia. The sample sizes of the studies ranged from 297 to 604 participants, employing various sampling techniques, with systematic random sampling being the most commonly used. The prevalence of hygiene practices varied between studies, with the highest prevalence reported by Shumi Bedada et al. at 55%, and the lowest reported by Habtam Ayenew Teshome et al. at 34%. These studies were conducted in both urban and rural areas, which may explain some of the differences in reported prevalence (see Table 1).

Meta-analysis
Pooled prevalence of hygiene practice during complementary feeding
Pooled prevalence of hygiene practice during complementary feeding
The overall pooled prevalence of HP was 42% (95% CI: 35%-48%, I2 = 92.34%, P < 0.001) using the random-effects model (Fig. 2).
Subgroup analysis
Subgroup analysis based on study area

High heterogeneity was observed between studies (I2 = 92.34%). Consequently, a subgroup analysis was conducted based on the study area. The pooled prevalence of hygiene practices during complementary feeding in southern Ethiopia was 41% (95% CI: 28-54%, I2 = 96.77%, p < 0.001), while the pooled prevalence for northern Ethiopia was 39% (95% CI: 33-45%, I2 = 80.5, p < 0.001) using the random-effects model (see Fig. 3).
Publication bias
Funnel plot to determine the presence of publication bias among 6 included studies

Publication bias was examined by the visual inspection of the funnel plot and it shows the presence of publication bias with the substantial asymmetry of the funnel plot (Fig. 4). However, we conduct objective Egger's test and Begs to confirm the presence of publication bias. As a result, Egger's test (p = 0.37), and Beg's test (p = 0.1329) showed no small study effect. To treat publication bias we ran the nonparametric trim-and-fill analysis, but no imputed studies were observed.

In this systematic review and meta-analysis, attitude and the presence of hand washing facilities near toilets were identified as significant factors associated with hygiene practices during complementary feeding. Analysis of studies revealed that respondents with a positive attitude toward hygienic practices were 2.7 times more likely (AOR: 2.7, 95% CI: 0.807:4.689, I2 = 0%, p < 0.001) to engage in good hygiene compared to those with a negative attitude. Additionally, respondents with hand washing facilities after toilet visits were 4.6 times more likely (AOR: 4.6, 95% CI: I2 = 31.4%, p = 0.01) to practice good hygiene during complementary feeding than those without such facilities (Table 4).
Discussion

This study estimated the pooled proportion of hygiene practices during complementary feeding among mothers with children aged 6 to 24 months in Ethiopia, which was found to be 42% (95% CI: 35%-48%). This aligns with findings from Bahir Dar Zuria, where similar attention to hygiene practices by policymakers and healthcare providers may have contributed to comparable results. However, the observed pooled proportion is higher than reported in comparable studies from Nigeria, where hygiene practice levels during complementary feeding were approximately 30%. Similarly, it is lower than findings from Uganda, which reported hygiene practice levels exceeding 50%. These differences highlight the influence of varying socioeconomic conditions, cultural practices, and infrastructure development across countries. Improved hygiene practices are crucial for child health, as they can influence nutritional outcomes and overall health. However, this proportion is higher than in the Tegedie district, likely due to regional differences in socioeconomic status and access to resources. Conversely, the pooled prevalence in this study was lower than the findings from the Bale Zone, highlighting regional disparities in complementary food hygiene practices.

Our study found that mothers with hand washing facilities near their toilets were more likely to practice good hygiene, consistent with the findings from Tegedie. These results emphasize the importance of access to proper sanitation facilities, which is particularly crucial in rural areas where hygiene resources may be limited. International comparisons suggest similar challenges in other low-income countries such as India, where limited access to hygiene infrastructure is a primary barrier to improved hygiene practices during complementary feeding. Such cross-country similarities further reinforce the need for globally coordinated efforts to improve water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) infrastructure. The disparities in hygiene practices between urban and rural areas can be attributed to varying levels of infrastructure development and resource availability. These findings are supported by similar studies from Kenya, which identified barriers such as limited resources and inadequate hygiene facilities. This cross-regional variation highlights the need for nuanced, context-specific interventions to bridge urban-rural gaps.

Additionally, mothers with positive attitudes toward hygiene were significantly more likely to adopt proper hygiene practices during complementary feeding. This aligns with studies from Ethiopia and Kenya, where positive attitudes were linked to better hygiene practices. This is further supported by evidence from Bangladesh, where behavior-change interventions focusing on mothers' attitudes significantly improved hygiene practices during complementary feeding. Such findings emphasize the importance of tailoring interventions to cultural contexts to maximize their effectiveness. These findings highlight the importance of education and awareness programs to improve hygiene behaviors, which are essential for child health.

In line with the WHO guidelines on Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF), this study provides insight into how hygiene practices during complementary feeding can be improved through better access to WASH facilities, as well as through behavior change interventions targeting mothers' attitudes. The evidence supports the need for integrated approaches that combine education on hygiene practices with improvements in infrastructure, especially in rural areas. In addition to improving WASH infrastructure, policymakers should focus on ensuring equitable access to sanitation facilities, especially in underserved areas, to facilitate better hygiene practices. Moreover, this study reinforces the global relevance of improving complementary feeding hygiene practices in line with WHO and UNICEF recommendations to reduce child morbidity and mortality associated with poor hygiene. Furthermore, these findings can inform policymakers and healthcare providers on the critical need for targeted programs addressing the factors that influence hygiene behaviors, including access to hand-washing facilities and the promotion of positive attitudes toward hygiene.

While this study provides valuable insights into hygiene practices in Ethiopia, it also has global relevance, especially for low-resource settings. The factors influencing hygiene practices during complementary feeding, such as access to infrastructure and maternal attitudes, are similar in many low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). By understanding the factors that influence hygiene practices during complementary feeding, this research can inform interventions aimed at improving maternal and child health outcomes in similar contexts worldwide. Future research should explore cross-country comparisons in greater detail, identifying shared challenges and opportunities for global policy alignment.
Strengths and limitations
Strengths
This study addresses a critical aspect of infant and young child feeding, focusing on hygiene practices during complementary feeding, which are crucial for child growth and development.
The systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines, ensuring a comprehensive and reliable synthesis of the available literature.
The rigorous inclusion criteria and quality assessments ensured that only relevant studies were included, which strengthens the validity of the findings.
Limitations

The study excluded qualitative research, which could have provided deeper insights into the determinants of hygiene practices. Future research could explore these factors using qualitative methods to uncover cultural and behavioral nuances that influence hygiene practices.

Restricting the review to articles published in English may have excluded relevant studies in other languages, potentially limiting the scope of the analysis. This limitation could be addressed by including studies in other languages in future reviews.

The exclusion of papers without full access may have resulted in the omission of relevant studies, potentially affecting the comprehensiveness of the findings. Additionally, the exclusion of grey literature based on eligibility criteria may have led to the omission of valuable studies, further limiting the scope of the review. Although grey literature was included in our search strategy, future reviews could consider broadening eligibility criteria to include a wider range of grey literature, which may capture additional insights typically not published in traditional academic journals.
Conclusion

This systematic review and meta-analysis revealed a low pooled proportion of hygienic practices during complementary feeding in Ethiopia. Key predictors of hygiene practices included maternal attitude and the availability of hand washing facilities near toilets. To address these issues, we recommend implementing training and counseling programs for mothers and caregivers on safe food processing and preparation. Further research should explore the impact of community-based interventions on improving hygiene practices and investigate the role of socio-economic and cultural factors in shaping these practices. Such insights can help inform targeted interventions to enhance food safety for infants.

passages.text: Ligand recognition by 14-3-3 proteins requires negative charges but not necessarily phosphorylation

Protein-protein interactions involving 14-3-3 proteins regulate various cellular activities in normal and pathological conditions. These interactions have mostly been reported to be phosphorylation-dependent, but the 14-3-3 proteins also interact with unphosphorylated proteins. In this work, we investigated whether phosphorylation is required, or, alternatively, whether negative charges are sufficient for 14-3-3epsilon binding. We substituted the pThr residue of pT(502-510) peptide by residues with a varying number of negative charges and investigated the binding of the peptides to 14-3-3epsilon using MD simulations and biophysical methods. We demonstrated that at least one negative charge is required for the peptides to bind 14-3-3epsilon, although phosphorylation is not necessary, and that two negative charges are preferable for high affinity binding. This discovery opens up new approaches for designing peptide-based 14-3-3 protein inhibitors.

Interactions of 14-3-3 proteins with their binding partners are attributed to phosphorylation of the binding partners. In this work, we show that at least one negative charge is required for the peptides to bind 14-3-3epsilon, although phosphorylation is not necessary, and that two negative charges are preferable for high affinity binding.

Protein phosphorylation, one of the most common post-translational modifications, plays an important role in the regulation of cellular functions. Protein kinases commonly phosphorylate seryl, threonyl, and tyrosyl residues of proteins, and this modification not only affects structural properties of the proteins but also their functions. Phosphorylation modulates protein-protein interactions, and some proteins recognize binding motifs containing phosphorylated amino acid residues.

14-3-3 proteins are a family of adapter proteins that are ubiquitously expressed in eukaryotic cells. The 14-3-3 proteins have many binding partners with a broad range of functions. Thus, these proteins are involved in various cellular activities in both physiological and pathological conditions. The 14-3-3epsilon isoform is upregulated and linked to abnormal cell growth in renal cancer. Reduced expression of 14-3-3epsilon has been reported in gastric cancer. The 14-3-3 proteins have also been associated with progression of larynx squamous cell carcinoma (LSCC), and small cell lung cancer. The 14-3-3 isoforms, epsilon, zeta, and gamma, are expressed and mislocalized to cytoplasm in cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), where a heterodimer of the epsilon with either zeta or gamma interacts with the cell cycle regulator, cell division cycle 25 A (CDC25A) to suppress apoptosis.

passages.text: It is widely reported that interactions between 14-3-3 proteins and their binding partners are through binding motifs comprising a phosphoseryl (pSer) or a phosphothreonyl (pThr) amino acid residues. The 14-3-3 proteins recognize two binding motifs, RSXpSXP and RXY/FXpSXP; pS is pSer, and X is any amino acid. Apoptosis signal-regulating kinase 1 (ASK1), Raf-1, CDC25A, cytosine-anenosine-adenosine-thymidine (CCAAT)-enhancer binding protein, and cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator are among the phosphorylated binding partners of 14-3-3 proteins. However, not all 14-3-3 interactions with their binding partners are phosphorylation-dependent, as they also bind proteins, such as CDC25B and exoenzyme S in a phosphorylation-independent manner.

Over the years, the binding mechanism of various phosphopeptides to 14-3-3 proteins has been studied using experimental and computational methods. Muslin et al. showed the phosphorylation-dependent binding of the Raf-1 derived peptide (pS-Raf-259) to 14-3-3zeta. The peptide occupies the amphipathic binding groove of 14-3-3zeta, and residues of the protein interacting with the peptide were identified, similar interaction were identified between 14-3-3zeta and phosphorylated myeloid leukemia factor 1 peptide. Furthermore, the human SOS1-derived peptide binds 14-3-3zeta in a similar manner as pS-Raf-259 does. In our previous work, we also developed CDC25A-derived phosphopeptides that bind 14-3-3epsilon, and we identified basic and aromatic amino acid residues (Lys50, Arg57, Arg130, and Tyr131) in the binding pocket of 14-3-3epsilon (Fig. 1) that interact with phosphorylated amino acid residues.

Ribbon structure of 14-3-3epsilon monomer. Top view (left), side view (right), and helices are labeled A-I, from N- to C-terminal. Helices that form the binding pocked are shown in orange. Amino acid residues of 14-3-3epsilon that interact with the phospharylated residue of the ligand are shown as stick.

Phosphorylation-independent interactions between 14-3-3 proteins and peptides have also been elucidated. R18, the unphosphorylated peptide that has two negatively charged amino acid residues, discovered by phage display designed for 14-3-3tau binding has been shown to interact with 14-3-3 proteins in a manner reminiscent of phosphorylated peptides, although R18 has additional hydrophobic interactions with the protein. Ottmann et al. demonstrated that the exoenzyme S-derived peptide interacts with 14-3-3 protein through ionic and hydrophobic interactions.

We have developed phosphopeptides that inhibit interactions between CDC25A and 14-3-3epsilon, and induce apoptosis of cSCC in animals. We further improved binding affinities of the peptides for 14-3-3epsilon by 6.5-fold. Although these phosphopeptides have high affinities for 14-3-3epsilon, it is likely that they are susceptible to dephosphorylation as various phosphatases have been shown to dephospharylate phosphopeptides in solution. Therefore, we proposed replacing the pThr residue of the parent peptide (pT(502-510)) with pThr mimics to potentially improve their resistance to phosphatases. It has long been known that 14-3-3 protein interactions with their binding partners are dependent on phosphorylation of the binding partner. Thus, we aimed to elucidate whether the binding of peptides is dependent on the presence of negatively charged amino acid residues, and not necessarily their phosphorylation.

Here, we studied binding between 14-3-3epsilon and peptide analogs in which the pThr residue in our previously studied peptide, pT(502-510), was substituted with residues carrying varying number of negative charges. We used biophysical methods to show that at least one negative charge is required for peptide binding to 14-3-3epsilon.
Materials and methods
Molecular dynamics simulations
Peptide-14-3-3epsilon complexes preparation

The starting structure was obtained from our previously studied 14-3-3epsilon-pT(502-510) complex. To obtain the various peptide analogs, pThr507 amino acid residue in the pT(502-510) was substituted with Thr, Glu, Gla, sThr, or Pmb amino acid residues (Fig. 2). Nonstandard residues were built in the YASARA program. Binding of the peptides to 14-3-3epsilon was studied using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations.

Structure of amino acid residues. Amino acid residues in position 507 of the peptide analogs have varying negative charge number from 0 to -2. Gla, gamma-carboxyglutamic acid residue; Glu, glutamic acid residue; Pmb, 2-amino-3-methyl-4-phosphonobutanoic acid residue; pThr, phosphothreonyl; sThr, sulfothreonyl; Thr, threonyl.
MD simulations of peptide-14-3-3epsilon complexes

Molecular dynamics simulations of the peptide-protein complexes were performed using the AMBER-FB15 force field as implemented in YASARA. Initially, the 14-3-3epsilon-peptide complex was solvated with water in a cubic simulation box with minimal distance of 1.2 nm between the edge of the box and the complex. Then, the system was energy minimized using standard parameters in YASARA. Then, the energy-minimized structures of 14-3-3epsilon-peptide complexes were solvated again with water molecules and 150 mm NaCl, and the structure of the system was simulated using md_run macro of YASARA. The 500 ns simulations were performed at 310 K and 1 atm pressure, and the trajectories were saved in xtc format that is compatible with GROMACS. The simulations were performed in two steps: (a) a 1 ns simulation using YASARA macro in the YASARA graphical user interface and (b) then, the simulation was continued in a computer background to generate a 499 ns trajectory using md_run macro of YASARA.
Trajectory analysis

Using YASARA, the first frames of the trajectories were converted to PDB format and used as topology files for analysis using analysis utilities of gromacs 2022.5. The trajectories were processed using trjconv module of gromacs. The rms module of GROMACS was used to calculate Calpha atoms root-mean-square deviation (RMSD). vmd software was used to calculate salt bridges and H-bonds between peptides and 14-3-3epsilon; 0.8 nm was used as the oxygen-nitrogen cutoff distance for salt bridges, and the donor-acceptor distance was set to 0.4 nm for H-bonds. The sasa module of GROMACS was used to calculate the solvent accessible surface area (SASA). The interfacial surface area (ISA) was calculated as follow:The van der Waals (VDW) surface area of residues were calculated using YASARA.
Peptides

The [sThr507]pT(502-510) peptide was from Biosynth International Inc. (Louisville, KY, USA), and other peptide analogs were synthesized in house. All N-alpha-Fmoc-protected amino acids were from CEM Corporation (Matthews, NC, USA), except N-alpha-(9-Fluorenylmethyloxycarbonyl)-gamma-Carboxy-l-glutamic-acid-gamma-di-t-butyl ester, (Fmoc-L-Gla(OtBu)2-OH), and (2S,3R)-2-((9-fluorenylmethyloxycarbonyl)amino)-4-(di-t-butylphosphonomethyl)-3-methylbutyric acid, (Fmoc-L-Pmb(tBu)2-OH) that were from Iris Biotech (Marktredwitz, Germany). Dimethylformamide (DMF) and N,N'-Diisopropylcarbodiimide (DIC) were from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA), the Rink amide ProTide resin and Oxyma Pure were from CEM (Matthews, NC, USA).
Peptide synthesis

The peptides were synthesized using CEM Liberty blue 2.0 microwave peptide synthesizer, in a 0.1 mmol scale on Rink amide ProTide resin using standard Fmoc chemistry with Boc, tBut, Bzl, and Pbf side chain protections. A 1-min Fmoc deprotection was carried out using 20% piperidine in DMF, and 2 min coupling was performed in DIC/Oxyma Pure at 90  C, except for the (Fmoc-L-Pmb(tBu)2-OH) that was coupled for 4 min. Peptide cleavage from the resin and side chains deprotection were simultaneously performed by stirring the peptide-resin in a cocktail containing TFA/Thioanisol/phenol/TIS/H2O/DODT in 81.5 : 5 : 5 : 1 : 5 : 2.5 (v/v/v/v/v/v) for 30 min on ice and then 3.5 h at room temperature. The resin was then separated from the cleavage cocktail by filtration, and the peptide was precipitated using ice-cold ether. Crude peptides were purified by reverse-phase HPLC using C8 column (Phenomenex (Torrance, CA, USA), Aeris 100 A, 5 mum, and 250 x 10 mm). A 0.1% TFA aqueous solution (v/v solvent A) and a 0.09% TFA acetonitrile (solvent B) were used to elute the peptides with a linear gradient of solvent B of 3-60% over 60 min at a flow rate of 4 mL min-1. Identities of the peptides were confirmed by Thermo Q-Exactive Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Table S1 and Figs S5-S8).
Differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF)

The (His)6-14-3-3epsilon was from Novus Biologicals (Centennial, CO, USA). Thermal unfolding of 14-3-3 protein and 14-3-3-peptide complexes were performed as previously described. Briefly, thermal unfolding was monitored using SYPRO-orange dye (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA) in Bio-Rad CFX384 Touch real-time PCR instrument (Hercules, CA, USA). The protein and protein-peptide complexes were dissolved in TRIS buffer (150 mm NaCl, 20 mm TRIS, 1 mm DTT, pH 7.4) to the final concentrations of 30 mum of peptide, 2 mum of 14-3-3epsilon, and 1000x dilution from SYPRO-Orange dye stock from the manufacturer. Melting temperature (T m) was determined from the first derivative of unfolding curve and change in melting temperature (DeltaT m) was calculated as the difference between T m of protein-peptide complex and T m of protein alone. At least three replicates were performed per peptide.
Surface plasmon resonance (SPR)

To obtain binding affinity (K D) of peptides for 14-3-3epsilon, SPR was performed as before. Briefly, recombinant (His)6-14-3-3epsilon was immobilized on activated Biacore NTA chip (Cytiva, Marlborough, MA, USA), at a flow rate of 5 muL min-1 for 10 min and then washed with the running buffer (20 mm Tris, 150 mm NaCl, 50 mum EDTA, 0.005% Tween 20, pH 7.4) for 20 min. Following protein immobilization, solutions of peptides were injected at increasing concentrations ranging from 4 to 500 mum (3.9, 7.8, 15.6, 31.2, 62.5, 125, 250 and 500 mum) for all analogs, except [Pmb507]pT(502-510) where concentrations ranging between 0.002 and 0.25 mum (0.002, 0.004, 0.008, 0.016, 0.031, 0.063, 0.125, and 0.25 mum) were used. The injections were carried out at a flow rate of 30 muL min-1 for 1 min, and dissociation time was 3 min in the running buffer. Steady-state affinities of the peptide were obtained by fitting the data using biacore insight evaluation Software ((Cytiva, Marlborough, MA, USA) version 5.0.18.22102). For each peptide, at least five replicates were done.
Results

In the present work, we elucidated the binding of peptide analogs of our previous studied peptide pT(502-510), in which the pThr amino acid residue in position 507 was substituted with amino acid residues with uncharged Thr, the singly charged sulfothreonine (sThr) and Glu, or with the doubly charged gamma-carboxyl glutamic acid(Gla) and 2-Amino-3-methyl-4-phosphonobutanoic acid (Pmb) residues (Table 1). Their chemical structures are shown in Fig. 2. The sThr is a phosphatase resistant pThr mimetic with one negative charge, and Pmb is a phosphatase resistant pThr mimetic with two negative charges. For comparison, pThr residue, in our published work, is also shown. Binding of each peptide analog to 14-3-3epsilon was computationally investigated in 500 ns MD simulations.

The Calpha atoms RMSD indicated that the peptides did not dissociate from 14-3-3epsilon-peptide complexes throughout simulations (Fig. S1). All 14-3-3epsilon-peptide complexes underwent structural rearrangement with RMSD between 0.15 and 0.4 nm, except the 14-3-3epsilon-[Gla507]pT(502-510) complex that had RMSD of 0.15-0.6 nm (Fig. S1). In all complexes, peptides showed less fluctuation than 14-3-3epsilon, except the [Pmb507]pT(502-510) peptide that showed higher fluctuation between 250 and 450 ns. Analysis of the interfacial surface area (ISA) between 14-3-3epsilon and peptide showed that the 14-3-3epsilon-peptide complexes had ISA of 13.7-17.3 nm2 (Table 1). The [Pmb507]pT(502-510) containing complex showed the largest ISA, while the [sThr507](502-510) containing complex had the smallest ISA. This suggests that all the peptides had a degree of interaction with 14-3-3epsilon during simulations. We further determined VDW surface area of the residue in position 507 of each peptide in each 14-3-3epsilon-peptide complexes. The results indicated that VDW surface area of the residues was between 1.386 and 1.954 nm2 (Fig. S2). The isosteric replacements, Pmb, Gla, and sThr residues had VDW surface area of 1.954, 1.824, and 1.816 nm2, respectively, and the nonisosteric replacements, Glu and Thr had VDW surface area of 1.605 and 1.386 nm2, respectively.

We identified several residues of the 14-3-3epsilon-peptide complex that interact with residues introduced in position 507 (Fig. 3 and Table S2). In the 14-3-3epsilon-[Thr507]pT(502-510) complex, no interactions involving Thr507 residue were observed. However, residues Arg502, Lys504, Ser505, Arg506, and Trp508 of the peptide formed H-bonds with residues Lys123, Glu134, Glu183, Asn176, Asp226, and Asn227 of 14-3-3epsilon (Table S2). In all other 14-3-3epsilon-peptide complexes, H-bonds were observed between the 507 residue of the peptides and Lys50, Arg57, Arg130, and Try131 of 14-3-3epsilon (Table S2). Pmb residue in the [Pmb507]pT(502-510) peptide formed the longest lasting H-bonds with these residues of 14-3-3epsilon, followed by Gla residue in [Gla507]pT(502-510). Additionally, Pmb formed H-bonds with Asn176, Leu175, Val179, and Leu223 (Fig. 3 and Table S2). The singly charged sThr and Glu in [sThr507]pT(502-510) and [Glu507]pT(502-510), respectively, showed less lasting H-bonds with Lys50, Arg57, Arg130, and Try131 residues of 14-3-3epsilon, than Gla and Pmb. Analysis of ionic interactions revealed no interactions between the 507 residues of the peptides with residues of the 14-3-3epsilon, except the Glu residue in [Glu507]pT(502-510) peptide that formed salt bridges with Lys50, Lys123, Arg130.

The binding of synthetic peptides to 14-3-3epsilon was initially assessed using DSF. The unfolding curves of 14-3-3-peptide complexes and 14-3-3epsilon, and their corresponding first derivatives are shown in Fig. 4 and Fig. S3. Analysis of DSF results indicated that [Pmb507]pT(502-510) peptide caused a DeltaT m of 14-3-3epsilon of 3.6  C, while all other peptides showed DeltaT m of 0.0  C. SPR was used to quantitatively determine K D of the peptides to 14-3-3epsilon. Figure 5 and Figure S4 show steady-state binding isotherm, and sensograms of the peptides binding to 14-3-3epsilon. [Pmb507]pT(502-510) peptide had the highest affinity of 0.009 +- 0.001 mum (Table 1).

Discussion

Interactions of 14-3-3 proteins with their binding partners have been primarily attributed to phosphorylated residues in the partners. However, 14-3-3 proteins have also been reported to bind proteins in phosphorylation-independent manner. Therefore, here we studied the role of negative charges in binding partners for interaction with 14-3-3epsilon. We showed that phosphorylation is not necessary for binding of 14-3-3epsilon, but single or double negative charges are required. We used MD simulations to determine the stability of 14-3-3epsilon-peptide complexes.

All the peptides formed stable complexes with 14-3-3epsilon; no peptide dissociation was observed (Fig. S1). The structural rearrangement was comparable to that of the phosphorylated peptides. ISA calculations can be used to reveal interactions between binding partners Our ISA results qualitatively confirmed that all the peptide had interactions with 14-3-3epsilon in the protein-peptide complexes. The Pmb residue of the highest affinity peptide, [Pmb507]pT(502-510), had the largest ISA, while the residues from nonbinding and weakly binding peptides had smaller ISA.

Since the residues of 14-3-3 proteins that interact with the phosphorylated amino acid residues of their binding partners are known, we sought to determine whether these interactions were maintained after residue substitutions in the parent peptide. In agreement with our previous results, analysis of H-bonds involving pThr507 residue in the 14-3-3epsilon-pT(502-510) complex confirmed that the residues interacted with Arg130, Tyr131, Arg57, and Lys50 for the most part of the simulation time (Table S2). As expected, the uncharged residue Thr in [Thr507]pT(502-510) did not interact with the reported residues of the 14-3-3epsilon (Table S2). H-bond analysis further showed that the singly charged residues sThr507 and Glu507 in [sThr507](502-510) and [Glu507]pT(502-510) peptides, respectively, exhibited short-lasting H-bonds with the residues, except the Arg130 residues that lasted for more than 85% of the simulation time. Gla507 of the [Gla507]pT(502-510) peptide interacted with Arg130 and Tyr131 for > 95% of the simulations time, but temporarily also interacted with Arg57 and Lys50. Like the pThr507, Pmb507 residue in [Pmb507]pT(502-510) peptide formed long-lasting interactions with all the four residues. The Pmb showed additional H-bonds with Asn176, Val179, Leu175, and Leu223. The H-bonds by residues in position 507 were formed by negatively charged side chain oxygen(s), and this explains why no H-bonds were detected with Thr507 residue of pT(502-510) peptide, as well as the more and longer lasting interaction by the doubly charged residues than the singly charged residue. Pmb residues and pThr have larger VDW surface area (Fig. S2), and subsequently larges ISAs, suggesting that besides charge, the larger of the side chain of residues in position 507 of the peptides might be of importance for the peptide binding to 14-3-3epsilon.

Differential scanning fluorimetry studies showed that the [Pmb507]pT(502-510) peptide caused a shift of 3.6  C, while other peptides did not cause any shift in T m of 14-3-3epsilon (Fig. S3) at 30 mum. The concentration at which the parent peptide and its other analogs caused change in T m of 14-3-3epsilon. The parent peptide, pT(502-510) shows DeltaT m of 3.7  C. Similar to DSF, in SPR experiments, the [Thr507]pT(502-510) did not bind 14-3-3epsilon at the studied concentrations (0-500 mum). This is in agreement with the fact that no interactions were observed between Thr507 residue of pT(502-510) peptide and residues of 14-3-3epsilon. This also indicates the crucial importance of negatively charged amino acid residues in peptide binders of 14-3-3epsilon. The [sThr507](502-510) and [Glu507]pT(502-510) had K D of 86.71 +- 8.07 mum and 141.75 +- 24.96 mum, respectively. The peptide containing the doubly charged Gla, [Gla507]pT(502-510) showed a higher affinity (K D of 24.06 +- 8.43 mum) (Table 1). Furthermore, the peptide with the doubly charged residue (Pmb) that has a phosphono group instead of phosphate group, [Pmb507]pT(502-510) showed the highest affinity (K D of 0.009 +- 0.001 mum) for 14-3-3epsilon than all other analogs. [Pmb507]pT(502-510) also has higher affinity for 14-3-3epsilon than our previously reported best binder for 14-3-3epsilon. The biophysical results are in agreement with our computational results showing stronger interactions between the [Pmb507]pT(502-510) peptide and 14-3-3epsilon. Similar to H-bond analysis, the [Gla507]pT(502-510) peptide showed weaker affinity than did [Pmb507]pT(502-510), yet both Gla and Pmb are doubly charged, and this could be due to different distributions of electrons on the side chain of these residues, resulting in different location of net charges, as well as the slight difference in their VDW surface areas.

Although binding of 14-3-3 with other proteins has been mostly reported with phosphorylated binding partners, it also interacts with unphosphorylated proteins like exoenzyme S, and unphosphorylated peptides. In a study conducted by Petosa et al. comparing binding of the unphosphorylated pan inhibitor of 14-3-3 proteins, R18 and the RAF-1 derived phosphopeptide pS-RAF-1-259, a crystal structure of 14-3-3zeta with R18 showed that a pentapeptide fragment of R18 (Trp-Leu-Asp-Leu-Glu) occupies binding site that overlaps with that of the phosphorylated peptides. The pentapeptide fragment contains two acidic amino acid residues (Asp and Glu), in the crystal structure, these residues are next to Lys49, Arg56, Arg60, and Arg127 residues of 14-3-3zeta, the phosphate group of pS-RAF-1-259 peptide is next to the same residues. In a different study on a peptide that contains two Asp residues, one Asp is located far (0.48-0.573 nm) from the basic residues of 14-3-3zeta to form significant interactions, the other Asp residue contacts Lys49. These studies are in agreement with our previous studies in which we reported similar residues (Lys50, Arg57, Arg130, and Tyr131) of 14-3-3epsilon to interact with the phosphorylated residue in our phosphopeptide analogs. The same residues of 14-3-3epsilon interacted with the 507 residues in the peptides presented in this work.

In the current work, we demonstrated that negative charge(s), not necessarily phosphorylation, are required for binding to 14-3-3 proteins and that two negative charges are favored for high affinity binding. The isosteric replacement of pThr with sThr with one negative charge on the side chain resulted in weak binder peptide. We also designed a peptide, [Pmb507]pT(502-510), having two negatively charged side chain, that has the highest, nanomolar, affinity for 14-3-3epsilon. In our previous work, we designed phosphopeptide analogs that inhibit squamous cell carcinoma cell growth. Unlike these pervious analogs, the [Pmb507]pT(502-510) is likely more stable, since it is not susceptible to dephosphorylation, making it a better candidate for inhibition of CDC25A-14-3-3epsilon interactions to promote apoptosis of cSCC cells.

passages.text: Effectiveness and safety of iGlarLixi in people with type 2 diabetes not at target on basal insulin and oral antidiabetic therapy in a prospective observational trial
Abstract
Aims

This study assessed efficacy and safety of the fixed ratio combination iGlarLixi 100/33 (insulin glargine 100 U/mL plus lixisenatide 33 mug/mL) in people with type 2 diabetes (PwT2D) in daily clinical practice.
Materials and Methods

This non-interventional, multicentre, prospective, single-arm 24-week study documented PwT2D with an HbA1c of 7.5%-10.0%, currently treated with a basal insulin supported oral therapy (BOT) in German primary care facilities, after the physician had decided to change treatment to iGlarLixi 100/33, independent of study participation. Primary end-point was the absolute change in HbA1c (%) from baseline.
Results

Of 93 participants included, 70 comprised the full analysis set for efficacy assessment. Approximately 24 weeks after switching to iGlarLixi 100/33 HbA1c (mean +- standard deviation) changed from 8.52 +- 0.82% by -0.74 +- 0.81% to 7.74 +- 0.76%, FPG from 174.3 +- 44.6 mg/dL (9.67 +- 2.48 mmol/L) by -32.9 +- 46.3 mg/dL (-1.83 +- 2.57 mmol/L) to 141.4 +- 34.1 mg/dL (7.85 +- 1.89 mmol/L) and body weight from 104.3 +- 22.5 kg by -3.0 +- 7.5 kg to 101.3 +- 21.6 kg (all p < 0.01). Furthermore, use of DPP4 inhibitors was significantly reduced from 34.8% to 6.8% of participants. Derived (from 7-point self-measured plasma glucose) time in range (TIR) increased and time above range (TAR) decreased after 24 weeks to target ranges (all p < 0.05). Flash glucose monitoring data of 20 patients showed similar patterns for TIR and TAR, respectively, and a reduction in time below range (p = 0.007). Hypoglycaemia events did not change significantly and were low in number. No severe hypoglycaemia was reported.
Conclusions

Modifying antiglycaemic treatment from a BOT regimen to iGlarLixi 100/33 in suboptimal controlled PwT2D in daily clinical practice improved glycaemic control without increasing hypoglycaemia and with favourable body weight change.
INTRODUCTION

Due to its progressive nature, type 2 diabetes (T2D) can become uncontrolled over time if necessary treatment advancement is inadequate or delayed, increasing the risk for long-term complications. Therapeutic inertia often begins with the use of one or more oral antidiabetic drugs (OADs) and generally continues when patients receive additional basal insulin (BI) therapy. The Standards of Diabetes Care and the German Practice Guideline strongly recommend timely advancement of basal insulin supported oral therapy (BOT), if glycaemic targets are not achieved. In addition, the German and the American Diabetes Association (ADA) recommend the use of fixed-ratio combinations (FRCs) of basal insulins and GLP-1 receptor agonists. Efficacy and safety of advancing treatment from a BOT to the FRC iGlarLixi (insulin glargine plus lixisenatide) has been demonstrated in the phase 3 study LixiLan-L, but how these trial results translate into daily clinical practice has not been systematically and prospectively assessed in Germany. Furthermore, time in (TIR), above (TAR) and below range (TBR), as well as glycaemic variability parameters, such as median and standard deviation (SD), derived from daily glucose profiles or flash glucose monitoring (FGM), are currently considered key factors in addition to HbA1c, that impact quality of life, micro- and macrovascular outcomes of people with T2D (PwT2D), helping improve treatment adherence and target achievement.

To this end, a prospective observational study, to assess glycaemic Control by modifying therapy witH iGlarLixi in the Suliqua  (30-60) pen in dAily practice in patieNts with type 2 diabetes whose blood sugar is not adequately Controlled on basal insulin and oral antidiabetic thErapy (CHANCE), investigated the effectiveness and safety of iGlarLixi in PwT2D suboptimal controlled on a BOT regimen in daily clinical practice.
METHODS
Study design and participants

CHANCE was a non-interventional, open-label, single-arm multicentre prospective trial with a 24-week observation period conducted across Germany. The trial received approval from the local ethics committee, was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and is registered at the ISRCTN registry (ISRCTN17541488, www.ISRCTN.org). All participants provided written informed consent. PwT2D suboptimal controlled with a BOT regimen (HbA1c 7.5-10.0% [58-86 mmol/mol]) were included after their treating physician had decided to change antiglycaemic treatment to an iGlarLixi 100/33 (insulin glargine 100 U/mL plus lixisenatide 33 mug/mL) regimen, independent from study participation. Patients aged <18 years, with type 1 diabetes, previous prandial insulin therapy, any contraindication for iGlarLixi, malignant disease, alcohol or drug abuse, dementia or inability to understand the content and objectives of the study were excluded. Patients and physicians had to have experience with the self-measured plasma glucose (SMPG) or FGM devices and associated software with no intention to change the device during the study.
Documentation

Data collection was done at baseline, and after 6 and 12 weeks of iGlarLixi 100/33 treatment via an electronic case report form. Self-measured fasting plasma glucose (FPG) values and iGlarLixi 100/33 doses were collected monthly. At baseline, physicians documented the HbA1c target individually defined for each patient as per local guidelines. HbA1c was measured every 3-6 months and SMPG profiles as well as (in a subgroup) FGM data over 14 days were documented at the main data collection time points, if available. At baseline and every 3 months, physicians asked their patients if any hypoglycaemia occurred during the previous 12 weeks and noted the reported events. All data had to be generated during daily clinical routine, and any therapeutic decision during the 24-week observation period was strictly left at the physician's discretion. Source data verification was performed at four (12.1%) sites. All results were validated after the end of data capture by conducting a data review.
Study end-points

Primary efficacy end-point was the absolute change of HbA1c [%] from baseline to 12 and 24 weeks, respectively. Secondary efficacy end-points included absolute change from baseline to 12 and 24 weeks, respectively, in self-measured FPG, iGlarLixi 100/33 dose, body weight (BW), body mass index (BMI), 7-point SMPG profiles and patient's treatment satisfaction (Diabetes Treatment Satisfaction Questionnaire, [DTSQ]) as well as target achievement rates within 1-12 and 1-24 weeks for FPG at target (<=110 mg/dL [<=6.1 mmol/L]) and HbA1c at individualised prespecified target. Safety end-points included hypoglycaemia incidence and events per patient-year, calculated for ADA level 1 (SMPG value of <70 and >=54 mg/dL [<3.9 and >=3.0 mmol/L]), ADA level 2 (SMPG value of <54 mg/dL [<3.0 mmol/L]) and ADA level 3 (severe hypoglycaemic event characterised by impaired mental and/or physical condition requiring outside assistance), as well as the respective nocturnal events (occurring between 10 PM-6 AM during sleep). Furthermore, incidence of adverse events (AEs), including adverse drug reactions (ADRs) and serious adverse events (SAEs), was assessed. For patients using FGM, absolute change from baseline to 12 and 24 weeks in TIR, TAR, TBR were secondary end-points. Post hoc, the percentage of derived TIR (dTIR), derived TAR (dTAR) and derived TBR (dTBR) from 7-point SMPG profiles, calculated as the number of glucose measurements per day between 70-180 mg/dL (3.9-10.0 mmol/L, dTIR), >180 mg/dL (>10.0 mmol/L, dTAR) and <70 mg/dL (<3.9 mmol/L, dTBR), divided by the number of all glucose measurements per day and multiplied with 100, were assessed.

passages.text: Statistical analysis

Efficacy and hypoglycaemia analyses were performed for the full analysis set (FAS) consisting of all participants who met inclusion criteria, provided written informed consent, received at least one dose of iGlarLixi (excluding off-label dose) during the study, switched to iGlarLixi 100/33 <2 weeks before and <1 week after study entry, and had HbA1c documented at baseline and at least once after baseline. Two subgroups of the FAS were predefined based on device used: FGM and SMPG. Analyses of hypoglycaemic events and AEs were also performed for the safety analysis set (SAS), that is, participants who had provided written informed consent and used iGlarLixi 100/33 at least once during the study. Categorical variables were expressed as frequency and continuous variables as mean plus-minus standard deviation (mean +- SD). All statistical tests were two-tailed with a significance level of 0.05 without adjustment for multiplicity. No adjustment for confounders was done. Comparisons of baseline with week 12 and 24 values for FPG, HbA1c, BW, BMI and iGlarLixi 100/33 doses were performed using paired t tests. For analysing hypoglycaemia incidence, 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using the Clopper-Pearson method. Comparisons between two (sub)groups were performed using Wilcoxon rank sum test and between more subgroups using Kruskal-Wallis test. Events per patient-year were calculated as the cumulative number of hypoglycaemic events available divided by the cumulative duration of iGlarLixi 100/33 therapy in years for all participants with treatment duration for each analysis window. Incidence of hypoglycaemia within the last 12 weeks prior to switching to iGlarLixi 100/33 was compared to the incidence of hypoglycaemia within the last 12 weeks prior to the end of week 12 and 24, respectively, using McNemar's test. Comparisons of baseline with week 24 values for the DTSQ status were performed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

To assess attrition bias, occurrence of any systematic differences in baseline characteristics from those who dropped out, those who were started off-label (i.e., not equal to 30 dose steps/day [DS/d] iGlarLixi 100/33, as approved in the European Union) and had to end their study participation and those who remained in the study was evaluated using Fisher's exact test. All analyses were performed using Statistical Analysis System version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA).
RESULTS
Patient characteristics

Data were collected between September 2020 and August 2022. Due to the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic, the original plan to document 250 participants at 100 centres could not be implemented. Of 111 participants enrolled, 92 were included in the analysis population. They were documented by 33 investigators (median [IQR]: 3 [1-3] patients per investigator), comprising a representative sample of German physicians, who usually care for BOT treated PwT2D (66.7% diabetologists/endocrinologists, 33.3% general practitioners/family physicians/internists). No significant differences in patient baseline characteristics, HbA1c target definition and insulin titration habits were observed between diabetologists/endocrinologists and general practitioners/family physicians/internists (data not shown). Reason for exclusion from SAS (n = 89) was no documented iGlarLixi 100/33 application (N = 3). Further reasons for exclusion from FAS (n = 70) were no HbA1c documentation after baseline (N = 8), off-label starting dose of iGlarLixi 100/33, that is,  30 DS/d (N = 10) or violation of other inclusion criteria (N = 1). Baseline characteristics, OAD treatment at baseline and previous BI therapy of the FAS population (n = 70), the off-label population (Off-label; n = 10) and for those who dropped out from FAS (Dropout; n = 8) are summarised in Table S1. Comparison of baseline parameters of the Off-label and Dropout groups with the FAS group showed no significant differences, except that fewer patients in the Off-label group received any OAD (70.0% vs. 95.7%; p = 0.024) and sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i; 50.0% vs. 10.0%; p = 0.020). Further information on diabetic late complications, concomitant diseases, lipidaemia and blood pressure is provided in Tables S2A and S2B, and on lipid-lowering and antihypertensive medication in Tables S3A and S3B, respectively. Baseline characteristics of FAS patients were as follows: age 64.6 +- 9.5 years, diabetes duration 12.3 +- 6.7 years, self-measured FPG 174.3 +- 44.6 mg/dL (9.67 +- 2.48 mmol/L), HbA1c 8.5 +- 0.8% (69 +- 8.7 mmol/mol), individualised target HbA1c 6.9 +- 0.4% (52 +- 4.4 mmol/mol), BW 104.3 +- 22.5 kg, BMI 35.1 +- 7.2 kg/m2 and 60.0% were male (Table 1). Main previously used BIs were insulin glargine 300 U/mL (41.4%) and 100 U/mL (34.3%; Table 1). Most common OADs were metformin (73.9%), SGLT2i (50.0%) and dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor (DPP-4i; 34.8%; Table 1 and Figure S1). The main reasons of the treating physicians for treatment modification with iGlarLixi 100/33 were expected improvement in glycaemic control, particularly HbA1c (100%), FPG (79%) and postprandial blood glucose (ppBG; 74%) and easy handling of the FRC (50%). Compared to SMPG patients, FGM patients were younger (60.3 vs. 66.4 years) and used more glinides (15.0% vs. 0%), had less arterial hypertension (70.0% vs. 94.0%), a trend to less renal failure (5.0% vs. 28.0%), and overall, less diabetic late complications (40.0% vs. 56.0%) and less concomitant diseases (80.0% vs. 94.0%) (Tables 1 and S2A).

Primary efficacy end-point

Starting at a baseline HbA1c level of 8.52 +- 0.82% (70 +- 9.0 mmol/mol; N = 70), mean changes from baseline to week 12 and 24 were -0.64 +- 0.78% (-7.0 +- 8.5 mmol/mol; N = 68; p < 0.0001) and -0.74 +- 0.81% (-8.1 +- 8.9 mmol/mol; N = 68; p < 0.0001), respectively, to a final average level of 7.74 +- 0.76% (61 +- 8.3 mmol/mol; N = 68) (Figure 1).

Secondary efficacy end-points

Self-measured FPG was significantly reduced from 174.3 +- 44.6 mg/dL (9.67 +- 2.48 mmol/L, N = 68) at baseline by -27.6 +- 48.2 mg/dL (-1.53 +- 2.68 mmol/L, N = 65; p < 0.0001) at week 12 and -32.9 +- 46.3 mg/dL (-1.83 +- 2.57 mmol/L, N = 62; p < 0.0001) at week 24, respectively, to 140.8 +- 33.7 mg/dL (7.81 +- 1.87 mmol/L, N = 64) at week 24 (Figure 2). Subgroups FGM and SMPG showed a slower HbA1c change 12 weeks after switching to iGlarLixi 100/33 with FGM use (-0.45%) versus SMPG (-0.71%), but similar total changes in HbA1c after 24 weeks (-0.70% vs. -0.76%; Figure 1). FPG baseline levels differed, but only numerically, between FGM (159.3 mg/dL [8.84 mmol/L]) and SMPG group (180.6 mg/dL [10.02 mmol/L]; p = 0.233; Table 1) as did changes at week 12 (by -17.2 vs. -32.3 mg/dL [-0.95 vs. -1.79 mmol/L]; p = 0.242) and week 24 (by -21.2 vs. -38.0 mg/dL [-1.18 vs. -2.11 mmol/L]; p = 0.379), respectively, resulting in comparable final FPG levels of 139.0 versus 142.5 mg/dL (7.71 vs. 7.91 mmol/L) (Figure 2). Within 24 weeks, HbA1c at predefined individual target (percentage [95% CI]) was achieved by 17.1% [9.2%; 28.0%] of patients, and a proportion of 30.0% [19.6%; 42.1%] achieved the FPG target, with slightly higher proportions for HbA1c (20.0% vs. 16.0%) and slightly lower for FPG in the FGM versus SMPG group (25.0% vs. 32.0%; data not shown).

Seven-point SMPG profiles consisted of preprandial and 2-h postprandial measurements before and after breakfast, lunch and dinner, respectively, and one measurement at bedtime. Documentations were available for 44-63% of participants. In these, significant reductions of plasma glucose levels at six of seven time points were observed from baseline to week 24 with changes leading to flatter mean daily glucose profiles in the FGM group versus SMPG group (Figure 3A-C and Table S4A-F).

After switch to iGlarLixi 100/33, metformin remained the main used OAD (72.5%), but use decreased to 66.1% after 24 weeks, driven by changes within the SMPG subgroup (Table S5). Use of SGLT2i remained stable at approximately 50%, while use of DPP-4i significantly decreased by 62% to 13.2% (p = 0.005) at switch, and to 6.8% after 24 weeks (p = 0.006; Figure S1 and Table S5). Use of sulfonylurea (SU) was low at baseline (2.9%) and remained low thereafter (Table S5). Percentage of patients using >=3 OADs decreased from 14.3% at baseline to 7.1% at switch and 6.8% after 24 weeks, while using no OAD increased from 4.3% at baseline to 14.3% at switch and to 20.3% after 24 weeks (p for row mean score differences at switch 0.0005 and after 24 weeks 0.0011; Table S6). Changes predominantly occurred in the SMPG group (Table S6).

BW at baseline was 104.3 +- 22.5 kg (N = 68); until week 12 and 24 it decreased significantly by -1.4 +- 5.4 kg (p = 0.048; N = 59) and -3.0 +- 7.5 kg (p = 0.002; N = 68), respectively (Table S7). BMI at baseline was 35.1 +- 7.2 kg/m2 (N = 68) and decreased significantly until week 12 and 24 by -0.5 +- 1.8 kg/m2 (p = 0.042; N = 59) and -1.0 +- 2.5 kg/m2 (p = 0.001; N = 68), respectively (Table S8).
Time in blood glucose ranges

In the FGM subgroup (n = 20), TIR increased significantly from baseline 56.5 +- 18.3% (N = 20) by 15.2 +- 16.4% (N = 16; p = 0.002) to a final average level of 74.5 +- 11.2% at week 24. TAR decreased significantly from baseline 36.5 +- 16.5% (N = 20) by -10.2 +- 13.6% (N = 16; p = 0.009) to 22.6 +- 10.3% at week 24, and TBR from 6.9 +- 8.1% (N = 20) by -4.4 +- 5.7% (N = 16; p = 0.007) to 3.5 +- 6.1% (Figure 4A and Table S9A).

In a post hoc analysis, derived time in blood glucose ranges was calculated from 7-point SMPG profiles for all patients with available data (N = 34). dTIR increased significantly from baseline 40.3 +- 31.4% (N = 34) by 32.3 +- 30.4% (N = 19; p < 0.001) to a final average level of 75.4 +- 23.5% (N = 25) at week 24. dTAR decreased significantly from baseline 59.7 +- 31.4% (N = 34) by -32.3 +- 30.4% (N = 19; p < 0.001) to 24.0 +- 22.9% (N = 25) at week 24, and dTBR changed from none (N = 34) to 0.6 +- 2.9% at week 24 (N = 25; Figure 4B and Table S9B). Comparing FGM and SMPG subgroups showed that baseline and final dTIR percentages were numerically higher and respective dTAR percentages were numerically lower with FGM versus SMPG (Figure 4B and Table S9B).
iGlarLixi 100/33 dose

Starting dose of iGlarLixi 100/33 at switch was 30.0 +- 0.0 DS/d (N = 70) as per European label for the (30-60) pen. iGlarLixi 100/33 was used once daily, mainly before dinner (45.7%) or before breakfast (40.0%). Until week 12 and 24, iGlarLixi 100/33 dose increased significantly by 10.1 +- 9.8 DS/d (N = 65; p < 0.001) and 11.1 +- 9.5 DS/d (N = 64; p < 0.001), respectively, resulting in a final dose of 41.1 +- 9.5 DS/d (N = 64). Final dose of previous BI was on average 38.7 +- 9.6 units per day (U/d), resulting in a dose difference of the BI component of iGlarLixi 100/33 at study end of approximately 2 U/d without differences in FGM versus SMPG group (Table S10). Final doses for each previous BI as well as iGlarLixi 100/33 final doses, stratified by FGM and SMPG subgroup, are provided in Table S10 and by previous BI in Table S11. Dose change frequency was 2.3 times per month (N = 53) during the first month, reducing to 1.8 (N = 63) and 1.6 times per month (N = 64) after 12 and 24 weeks, respectively.
Hypoglycaemia

Incidence and events per patient-year within the last 12 weeks before, and 12 and 24 weeks, respectively, after switching to iGlarLixi 100/33 for ADA level 1, 2 and 3 hypoglycaemia are shown in Tables S12A-C. Overall, incidences and events per patient-year were low for a T2D population treated with BOT and did not change significantly after modifying treatment with the FRC iGlarLixi 100/33. No severe hypoglycaemia (ADA level 3) was reported during the entire study.
Patient reported outcomes

Treatment satisfaction status sum score at baseline was 24.2 +- 7.7 (N = 66), which increased significantly by 5.2 +- 8.3 (N = 60) to 29.6 +- 5.9 (N = 61) at week 24 (p < 0.001); improvement was slightly greater for FGM (6.9 +- 4.5 [N = 20]) versus SMPG subgroup (4.4 +- 9.6 [N = 40]; Tables S13A,B). The status scores for perceived frequency of hyperglycaemia and hypoglycaemia at baseline were 3.8 +- 1.4 and 0.9 +- 1.2 (N = 66), respectively; only perceived hyperglycaemia decreased significantly by -1.3 +- 1.7 (N = 59) to 2.5 +- 1.6 (N = 60; p < 0.001) at week 24 (Table S14). Treatment satisfaction change sum score was 11.7 +- 6.1 (N = 59); improvement was slightly lower for FGM (9.5 +- 4.7 [N = 19]) versus SMPG subgroup (12.8 +- 6.5 [N = 40]; Tables S13A,B). Perceived hyperglycaemia and hypoglycaemia change scores were -0.9 +- 1.7 and -1.2 +- 1.6 (N = 61), respectively, with greater changes seen in the FGM (-1.9 +- 0.7 and -1.3 +- 1.3 [N = 20]) versus SMPG subgroup (-0.4 +- 1.8 and -1.1 +- 1.8 [N = 41]; Table S14).
Safety
Table S15 shows the incidence of AEs, ADRs and SAEs, reported for patients in SAS (n = 89) over 24 weeks.
DISCUSSION

Switching the BI in BOT regimens to iGlarLixi and Gla-100, respectively, in the randomised, open-label phase 3 trial LixiLan-L provided improved glycaemic control in adult PwT2D, with beneficial effects on BW and at a similar risk of overall hypoglycaemia from baseline to week 30 with iGlarLixi. The present prospective observational study CHANCE was designed to evaluate if the beneficial effects of iGlarLixi found in LixiLan-L translate into conditions of real world use. Baseline values regarding diabetes duration were comparable to those documented in LixiLan-L. However, our study participants were approximately 5 years older, with higher BW, BMI, HbA1c and FPG levels, and final dose of previous BI, with more male participants. Previous BI in LixiLan-L included Gla-100, IDet and neutral protamin Hagedorn (NPH) insulin, while previous BI in CHANCE included Gla-300, Gla-100, IDet and IDeg. In the real world evidence (RWE) trials STAR.Ro and SoliSimplify BB, and a RWE pooled analysis, separately evaluating BOT or OAD treated patients with T2D switching to iGlarLixi, within the BOT study arm, age, diabetes duration, FPG, previous insulin glargine and metformin use were comparable to CHANCE, whereas CHANCE participants showed fewer females, lower baseline HbA1c,  lower use of SU and higher DPP-4i and SGLT2i use. The very low use of SU (2.9%) observed in our study was comparable to findings in STAR.Ro study, and lower than in older non-interventional studies on BOT patients conducted in Germany (13.5% and 10.7%), supporting a trend to less use of SU over the past years in Germany, and in line with ADA guidelines, which support less use of SU, while the German National Healthcare Guideline lists SU as an equivalent therapy to other OADs in PwT2D without cardiovascular risk. The use of DPP-4i was markedly reduced in our study from 34.8% to 13.2% when starting iGlarLixi treatment and further reduced to 6.7% after 12 weeks of treatment. In the real world study ENSURE-ADR DPP-4i use was lower at baseline (10%) and was reduced to 1% when starting iGlarLixi, which is closer to the recommendations in the European iGlarLixi label. Comparison of four participants still on DPP-4i versus 20 participants that stopped DPP-4i in our study revealed higher HbA1c levels at baseline (9.03 +- 1.08% vs. 8.46 +- 0.81% [75 +- 11.8 vs. 69 +- 8.9 mmol/mol]) with greater changes (-1.03 +- 0.96% vs. -0.63 +- 0.77% [-11.3 +- 10.5 vs -6.9 +- 8.4 mmol/mol]) to 8.00 +- 0.55 versus 7.71 +- 0.69% [64 +- 6.0 vs. 61 +- 7.5 mmol/mol] after 24 weeks (data not shown), suggesting that the DPP-4i were maintained in expectation of a better HbA1c reduction. The group of 70 participants included in the FAS represents PwT2D for whom the recommended treatment modification with a FRC should be considered.

CHANCE demonstrated glycaemic improvement in daily practice with a clinically meaningful change in HbA1c, although less at 24 weeks than that observed at 30 weeks in LixiLan-L (-0.7% vs. -1.1%), with higher baseline levels. However, in LixiLan-L patients entered a run-in period of 6 weeks for BI treatment optimisation and only a selection of those with FPG <=140 mg/dL (<=7.8 mmol/L) entered the study. HbA1c reduction in CHANCE after 24 weeks was also less versus STAR.Ro (-1.0%), but similar to SoliSimplify BB, both starting and ending at higher values versus CHANCE. In addition, an RWE pooled analysis showed higher HbA1c reductions (-1.3%) but resulted in similar HbA1c levels after 24 weeks. Reductions in FPG were significant in CHANCE but ended around 140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L), which is in line with the final values found in other RWE studies. In randomised clinical trials, such as LixiLanL, mean final FPG was 122 mg/dL (6.8 mmol/L), demonstrating that titration after 24 weeks is incomplete in real world use. In fact, final mean iGlarLixi dose in LixiLan-L was 47 DS/d compared to 41 DS/d in CHANCE, 45 DS/d in STAR.Ro and 36 DS/d in RWE pooled analysis, respectively. Of note, titration was started and continued more slowly than recommended by clinical trials, once every 1 to 2 weeks in the first month after switching to iGlarLixi and then reduced to once every 2 to 3 weeks. Titration frequency might have been reduced too early in CHANCE, given that only one-sixth of patients reached their individual HbA1c target and less than one-third achieved FPG targets. On the other hand, slow titration appears to reduce the risk of hypoglycaemia to very low incidence and events per patient-year as observed in CHANCE and other real world studies on glargine-based therapies, and to enable the development of the blood glucose lowering potential of iGlarLixi. This is in line with the observed significant lowering and flattening of the 7-point SMPG profiles and TIR, TAR and TBR, derived from SMPG profiles, as well as from FGM data, being within the recommended ranges of TIR (>70%), TAR (<25%) and TBR (<4%), which corresponds to the results from other studies using CGM in insulin-naive patients starting with iGlarLixi treatment. dTIR, dTAR and dTBR can be used to provide a picture of glycaemic variability, if FGM data are not available. Both glycaemic ranges, derived from FGM and SMPG data, consistently showed significant improvements with iGlarLixi. The results on time in glycaemic ranges derived from SMPG data are in line with those obtained post hoc from SMPG data of the LixiLan-L-CN study with Chinese participants. Of note, TAR was reduced and TIR was increased more pronounced in the FGM group versus SMPG group. Moreover, FGM use revealed that more hypoglycaemic episodes occurred than reported by the patients, and that these were significantly reduced below the recommended threshold of <4% after switching to iGlarLixi. At baseline, FGM use was accompanied by less late complications and less concomitant diseases versus SMPG use; however, the FGM group was on average 6 years younger than the SMPG group.

Another FRC, consisting of insulin degludec and liraglutide (iDegLira), was assessed in retrospective chart review studies and a prospective real world analysis in BOT patients, showing a greater HbA1c reduction of approximately 1% versus 0.7% in our study, but with only approximately 1 kg weight loss versus 3 kg in our study. In a recent review of both FRCs the authors conclude that both FRCs have better effect on glycaemic control than basal insulin up-titration strategies and similar effects compared to initiation of a basal-bolus regimen, mitigating their side effects including the risk of hypoglycaemia, weight gain or gastrointestinal adverse effects, with very different pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties due to differences in both components not allowing to state if one is better than the other. Our study findings support the concept of combining a predominantly prandial acting GLP-1 RA component with a basal acting basal insulin as an effective and safe treatment modification alternative for BOT regimens to BOT plus once daily prandial insulin, premix or basal-bolus insulin treatment regimens.

The observed improvements in glycaemic control in our study were accompanied by a significant improvement in treatment satisfaction score and reductions in perceived frequency of hyperglycaemia, supporting the improvements in patient-reported outcomes found in SoliMix study.

Major limitations of the present study were the lack of randomisation and a comparator arm, as well as 21% loss to follow-up, which might have introduced selection bias. A comparator would have been the FRC iDegLira, which is not available in Germany due to reimbursement issues. Therefore, this study had to be conducted in a single-arm design. Also, more patients on BOT could have been included, if the second dosage form, iGlarLixi 100/50, were also available in Germany, which is not the case for reimbursement reasons. In this respect, we were also unable to investigate the use of iGlarLixi 100/50 in German daily clinical practice. However, pre-post comparisons before and after switching to iGlarLixi 100/33 were feasible, and analyses of dropout and off-label starting dose patients with FAS patients have shown no clinically relevant differences between these groups. Another limitation is that part of the effects observed might be attributable to the Hawthorne effect. In addition, a contribution of factors other than the switch to iGlarLixi 100/33 to the results cannot be excluded, since, for example, the administration of DPP-4i was largely discontinued, resulting in a reduced number of OADs used. Lastly, patients were voluntarily enrolled and prospectively followed, which might have influenced their behaviour. Therefore, the present results might not be fully representative for all PwT2D switching their BI to iGlarLixi 100/33.

In conclusion, modifying antiglycaemic treatment to iGlarLixi 100/33 in PwT2D insufficiently controlled on BOT regimens in German primary care settings was effective at reducing FPG, ppBG and HbA1c levels, and allowed patients to reach glycaemic target ranges without increasing hypoglycaemia and with favourable BW change.
